1. This thought also helps to remove the desire for empty fame: it is no longer in your power to have lived your whole life, or at least your life since youth, as a philosopher. Many others can see plainly, and so can you, that you are far from philosophy. So you have fallen into confusion, and it is no longer easy for you to win the reputation of a philosopher; and the way your life is set up works against it too. If, then, you have truly seen where the matter lies, throw away the thought of how you will look to others, and be content if you live the rest of your life in the way your nature wants. Pay attention, then, to what it wants, and let nothing else distract you. For you have wandered down many paths and found happiness nowhere—not in logical arguments, not in wealth, not in reputation, not in enjoyment, not anywhere. Where is it, then? In doing what human nature requires. And how is a person to do this? By having principles from which his impulses and his actions come. What principles? Those about good and bad: the belief that nothing is good for a human being that does not make him just, self-controlled, courageous and free; and that nothing is bad that does not do the opposite.

2. Whenever you do anything, ask yourself: How does this affect me? Will I regret it? A little while and I am dead, and everything is gone. What more do I want, if what I am doing now is the work of an intelligent living being, a being made for community, and one who lives under the same law as God?

3. Alexander and Caius and Pompeius—what are they compared with Diogenes and Heraclitus and Socrates? For these men understood things, and their causes, and the matter they are made of; and their ruling faculties were in keeping with what they pursued. But as for the others, how many things they had to worry about, and to how many things they were slaves!
4. Remember that people will go on doing the same things all the same, even if you burst with anger.

5. This is the chief thing: do not be disturbed, for everything happens according to the nature of the universe; and in a little while you will be no one and nowhere, like Hadrianus and Augustus. Next, fix your eyes steadily on the task in front of you and look at it. Remember at the same time that it is your duty to be a good person, and remember what human nature asks of you; then do that without turning aside. And speak as seems most just to you—only let it be with goodwill, with modesty, and without hypocrisy.

6. The nature of the universe has this work to do: to move what is here over there, to change things, to take them up from here and carry them there. Everything is change; yet there is no need to fear anything new. Everything is familiar to us; and the way things are shared out still remains the same.

7. Every nature is content with itself when it goes well on its way. A rational nature goes well on its way when, in its thinking, it agrees to nothing false or uncertain; when it directs its impulses only toward acts that serve the common good; when it limits its desires and aversions to the things that are in its power; and when it is satisfied with everything the common nature assigns to it. For every particular nature is a part of this common nature, as the nature of a leaf is part of the nature of the plant. The difference is that the leaf's nature is part of a nature that has no perception or reason and can be obstructed; but a human being's nature is part of a nature that cannot be obstructed, and that is intelligent and just. For that common nature gives to each thing its span of time, its substance, its cause, its activity, and what happens to it, in equal shares and according to the worth of each. But when you examine this, do not look for any one thing to be equal in every respect to any other single thing. Instead, take all the parts of one thing together and compare them with all the parts of another taken together.

8. You have no time to read. But you have time to curb arrogance; you have time to rise above pleasure and pain; you have time to rise above the love of fame, and not to be angry with stupid and ungrateful people—and even to care for them.
9. Let no one hear you complaining any longer about life at court, or about your own life.

10. Regret is a kind of self-reproach for having neglected something useful. But what is good must be something useful, and the perfectly good person should care about it. Yet no such person would ever regret having turned down a sensual pleasure. So pleasure is neither good nor useful.
11. This thing: what is it in itself, in its own makeup? What is its substance and material? What is its causal nature, or form? What is it doing in the world? And how long does it last?

12. When you are reluctant to get up from sleep, remember that doing acts that serve the community is in keeping with your own makeup and with human nature, while sleep is something we share even with animals that lack reason. And what is in keeping with each creature's own nature is also more truly its own, better suited to its nature, and indeed more pleasing too.
13. Constantly, and if possible with every impression that comes to your soul, apply to it the principles of physics (the study of nature), of ethics, and of logic.

14. Whenever you meet anyone, say to yourself at once: What opinions does this person hold about good and bad? For if he holds such and such opinions about pleasure and pain and what causes each, about fame and disgrace, about death and life, then it will not seem surprising or strange to me if he does such and such things; and I shall remember that he is compelled to act this way.

15. Remember: just as it is shameful to be surprised when a fig tree bears figs, so it is shameful to be surprised when the world produces the things it naturally produces. And it is shameful for a doctor to be surprised when someone has a fever, or for a ship's pilot to be surprised when the wind is against him.

16. Remember that changing your mind and following someone who corrects your mistake is just as much in keeping with your freedom as persisting in your mistake. For the activity is your own: it is carried out by your own impulse and your own judgment, and indeed by your own understanding too.

17. If something you find fault with is in your own power, why do you do it? And if it is in someone else's power, whom do you blame—the atoms, that is, chance, or the gods? Both are foolish. You must blame no one. If you can, correct the cause; if you cannot do that, at least correct the thing itself; and if you cannot do even that, what use is it to you to find fault? For nothing should be done without a purpose.

18. What has died does not fall out of the universe. If it stays here, it also changes here, and is broken up into its own parts, which are the elements of the universe and of yourself. And these too change, and they do not grumble.

19. Everything exists for some purpose—a horse, a vine. Why does that surprise you? Even the sun will say, "I exist for a purpose," and the rest of the gods will say the same. What, then, do you exist for? To enjoy pleasure? See whether common sense allows that.

20. In everything, nature has taken thought for the ending no less than for the beginning and the time it lasts, just like someone who throws a ball into the air. What good is it to the ball to be thrown up, or what harm to come down, or even to have fallen? And what good is it to a bubble to hold together, or what harm to burst? The same can be said of a lamp's flame too.

21. Turn the body inside out and see what sort of thing it is; and what it becomes when it grows old, and when it is diseased. Short-lived are the one who praises and the one who is praised, the one who remembers and the one who is remembered. And all this happens in a small corner of this part of the world; and even here people do not all agree with one another—no, no one even agrees with himself. And the whole earth, too, is a mere point.
22. Pay attention to what is in front of you, whether it is an opinion, an act, or a word. You deserve what you are suffering: you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.

23. Am I doing something? I do it for the good of humankind. Does something happen to me? I accept it and trace it back to the gods, and to the source of all things, from which everything that happens comes.
24. What bathing looks like to you—oil, sweat, dirt, filthy water, everything disgusting—that is what every part of life is like, and everything.

25. Lucilla saw Verus die, and then Lucilla died. Secunda saw Maximus die, and then Secunda died. Epitynchanus saw Diotimus die, and then Epitynchanus died. Antoninus saw Faustina die, and then Antoninus died. Everything is like this. Celer saw Hadrianus die, and then Celer died. And those sharp-witted men, whether seers or men puffed up with pride—where are they? Where are the sharp-witted Charax, and Demetrius the Platonist, and Eudaemon, and anyone else like them? All of them lasted only a day; all long dead. Some were not remembered even for a short time; others have become figures in legends; and others again have vanished even from the legends. Remember this, then: this little compound that is you must either be broken up, or your poor breath must be put out, or else it must be moved and placed somewhere else.

26. It brings a person satisfaction to do the proper work of a human being. And the proper work of a human being is to be kind to his own kind, to think little of the stirrings of the senses, to judge rightly the impressions that seem convincing, and to study the nature of the universe and the things that happen in it.
27. You have three relationships: one to the body that encloses you; a second to the divine cause from which everything comes to everyone; and a third to those who live alongside you.

28. Pain is either an evil to the body—in which case let the body say what it thinks of it—or to the soul. But the soul has the power to keep its own calm and peace, and not to judge that pain is an evil. For every judgment, every impulse, every desire and every aversion is within, and no evil climbs up that high.

29. Wipe out the impressions in your mind by often saying to yourself: "It is in my power now to keep this soul free of all badness, of desire, and of any disturbance at all. Rather, looking at all things, I see what their nature is, and I use each one according to its worth." Remember this power, which nature has given you.
30. Speak in the senate and to every person, whoever he may be, fittingly and without putting on airs. Use plain speech.

31. Augustus's court: his wife, his daughter, his descendants, his ancestors, his sister, Agrippa, his relatives, his close companions, his friends; Areius, Maecenas, his doctors and his sacrificing priests—the whole court is dead. Then turn to the others. Consider not the death of a single person but the death of a whole family, such as the family of the Pompeii; and consider the words inscribed on tombs: "The last of his line." Then think how hard the people before them worked to leave an heir; and then that, of necessity, someone has to be the last. Here again, consider the death of a whole family line.

32. It is your duty to put your life in good order one act at a time; and if each act does its duty as far as possible, be content. No one can stop you from making each act do its duty. "But something from outside will stand in the way." Nothing will stand in the way of your acting justly, with self-control, and with good sense. "But perhaps some other kind of activity will be hindered." Well, if you accept the hindrance calmly and are content to turn your efforts to what is allowed, another opportunity for action is at once put before you in place of the one that was hindered. And it is one that will fit into the ordering of life we are speaking of.
33. Receive wealth or prosperity without arrogance; and be ready to let it go.

34. If you have ever seen a hand cut off, or a foot, or a head, lying somewhere apart from the rest of the body—that is what a person makes of himself, as far as he can, when he is not content with what happens, and cuts himself off from others, or does anything that sets him against others. Suppose you have broken away from the natural unity—for you were made by nature as a part, but now you have cut yourself off. Still, here is a beautiful provision: it is in your power to join yourself to it again. God has allowed no other part to come back together once it has been separated and cut away. But consider the kindness with which he has honored human beings: he has put it in their power not to be separated from the whole at all; and when they have been separated, he has allowed them to return, to be united with it again, and to take up their place as a part once more.

35. Just as the nature of the universe has given each rational being all the other powers it has, so we have also received from it the following power. The nature of the universe takes everything that stands in its way and opposes it: it turns each such obstacle around, fixes it in its destined place, and makes it part of itself. In the same way, a rational being is able to make every obstacle into material for itself, and to use it for whatever purpose it may have set out to achieve.

36. Do not upset yourself by picturing your whole life at once. Do not let your thoughts take in, all together, all the various troubles you may expect to happen to you. Instead, each time one comes, ask yourself: What is there in this that is unbearable and beyond enduring? You will be ashamed to admit it. Next, remember that it is neither the future nor the past that weighs on you, but only the present. And the present shrinks to very little if you only mark off its limits, and if you scold your mind when it cannot hold out against even this much.

37. Do Panthea or Pergamus sit by the tomb of Verus now? Does Chaurias or Diotimus sit by the tomb of Hadrianus? That would be ridiculous. Well, suppose they did sit there: would the dead know it? And if the dead knew it, would they be pleased? And if they were pleased, would that make them immortal? Was it not fated that these mourners too would first become old women and old men, and then die? And once these mourners were dead, what would the dead do then? All this is foul smell and blood in a bag.
38. "If you can see sharply, look and judge wisely," says the philosopher.
39. In the makeup of a rational being I see no virtue that stands opposed to justice; but I do see a virtue that stands opposed to the love of pleasure, and that is self-control.

40. If you take away your opinion about whatever seems to be causing you pain, you yourself stand completely safe. "Who is this 'yourself'?" "Reason." "But I am not reason." "So be it. Then let reason itself not trouble itself. And if some other part of you is suffering, let that part form its own opinion about itself."

41. Whatever hinders perception by the senses is bad for an animal's nature. Whatever hinders its impulses—its desires—is equally bad for an animal's nature. And in the same way, something else hinders plants and is bad for their makeup. So, then, whatever hinders the intelligence is bad for an intelligent nature. Apply all this to yourself, then. Does pain or physical pleasure lay hold of you? That is for the senses to look to. Has some obstacle blocked you while you were striving toward something? If you were striving for it unconditionally, without any reservation, then this obstacle really is bad for you as a rational being. But if you took into account how things usually go, you have not yet been harmed, or even hindered. As for the things that belong properly to the understanding, no one else is in the habit of hindering them; for neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant, nor insults can touch the understanding in any way. Once the understanding has become a sphere, it stays a sphere.
42. It is not right for me to cause myself pain, for I have never deliberately caused pain even to anyone else.

43. Different things delight different people; my delight is to keep my ruling faculty sound: not turning away from any person, or from anything that happens to people, but looking at everything and receiving it all with welcoming eyes, and using each thing according to its worth.

44. Make sure you take hold of this present time for yourself. For those who would rather chase fame after death do not stop to think that the people of later times will be just like these people they cannot stand now; and both are mortal. And what is it to you, in any way, if these later people utter this or that sound, or hold this or that opinion about you?

45. Take me and throw me wherever you like. For there I shall keep the divine spirit within me calm—that is, content—so long as it can feel and act in keeping with its own proper makeup. Is this change of place reason enough for my soul to be unhappy and worse off than before—cast down, swelling up, shrinking back, frightened? And what will you find that is reason enough for that?

46. Nothing can happen to any human being that is not the kind of thing that happens to human beings; nothing to an ox that is not in keeping with the nature of an ox; nothing to a vine that is not in keeping with the nature of a vine; nothing to a stone that is not proper to a stone. If, then, what happens to each thing is both usual and natural, why should you complain? For the common nature brings you nothing that you cannot bear.

47. If you are pained by something outside you, it is not that thing that troubles you, but your own judgment about it. And it is in your power to wipe that judgment out right now. But if something in your own character pains you, who is stopping you from correcting your opinion? And even if you are pained because you are not doing some particular thing that seems right to you, why not act instead of complaining? "But what if some obstacle too strong for me is in the way?" Then do not be grieved, for the reason it is not being done does not depend on you. "But life is not worth living if this cannot be done." Then leave life contentedly, just as someone dies who is still in the midst of his work—and leave it well pleased, too, with the things that stand in your way.

48. Remember that the ruling faculty cannot be conquered when it gathers itself together and is satisfied with itself, as long as it does nothing it does not choose to do, even when its resistance is mere stubbornness. What, then, will it be like when it judges something with the help of reason and after careful thought? That is why a mind free from passions is a fortress: a human being has nothing more secure to run to for refuge, where from then on he cannot be captured. Whoever has not seen this is ignorant; but whoever has seen it and does not run to this refuge is unhappy.

49. Tell yourself nothing beyond what your impressions report at first sight. Suppose you have been told that someone is speaking badly of you. That much has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported. I see that my child is sick. That I do see; but that he is in danger, I do not see. So always keep to what appears at first sight, and add nothing to it yourself from within; then nothing happens to you. Or rather, do add something—but add it as someone familiar with everything that happens in the world.

50. A cucumber is bitter: throw it away. There are briars in the road: step aside from them. That is enough. Do not go on to add, "And why were such things made in the world?" For someone who understands nature would laugh at you, just as a carpenter and a shoemaker would laugh at you if you found fault because you saw in their workshop the shavings and scraps from the things they make. And yet they have places where they can throw away those shavings and scraps, while the nature of the universe has no space outside itself. The wonderful thing about nature's art is that, although she has set limits around herself, she takes everything within her that seems to be decaying, growing old and useless, changes it into herself, and makes new things again out of these very same materials. So she needs no material from outside, and no place into which to throw what decays. She is content, then, with her own space, her own matter, and her own art.

51. Do not be sluggish in what you do, or muddled in what you say, or wandering in your thoughts. Do not let your soul be at war with itself within, or spill out of itself. And do not be so busy in life that you have no leisure. Suppose people kill you, cut you to pieces, curse you. How can any of this stop your mind from staying pure, wise, sober and just? It is as if someone stood beside a clear, pure spring and cursed it: the spring never stops sending up drinkable water. And if he throws mud or filth into it, it will quickly scatter them and wash them out, and will not be polluted at all. How, then, will you have a spring that never runs dry, and not a mere well? By shaping yourself, every hour, toward freedom—together with contentment, simplicity and modesty.

52. Whoever does not know what the world is does not know where he is. And whoever does not know what the world exists for does not know who he is, or what the world is. And whoever has failed to know any one of these things could not even say what he himself exists for. What, then, do you think of someone who avoids or seeks the praise of people who applaud—people who know neither where they are nor who they are?

53. Do you want to be praised by someone who curses himself three times an hour? Do you want to please someone who does not please himself? Does anyone please himself who regrets nearly everything he does?

54. Do not let your breathing any longer be the only thing in tune with the air around you; let your intelligence now also be in harmony with the intelligence that embraces all things. For that intelligent power is spread through every part and runs through all things for anyone willing to draw it in, no less than the power of the air is there for anyone able to breathe it.

55. In general, wickedness does no harm at all to the universe; and in particular, one person's wickedness does no harm to another. It harms only the one person who has the power to be free of it as soon as he chooses.

56. To my own free will, my neighbor's free will is neither good nor bad—no more than his poor breath and flesh are. For even though we are made above all for the sake of one another, still the ruling faculty of each of us has its own proper work. Otherwise my neighbor's wickedness would be my harm; and God has not willed this, because he did not want my unhappiness to depend on someone else.

57. The sun seems to be poured down, and it does indeed spread out in every direction, yet it is not poured away. For this spreading is a stretching out. That is why its rays are called aktines, "extensions": in Greek the name comes from their being stretched out, apo tou ekteinesthai. You can judge what kind of thing a ray is if you watch sunlight coming through a narrow opening into a darkened room. It stretches out in a straight line, and it is, as it were, broken off when it meets some solid body that stands in its way and cuts off the air beyond. But there the light stays fixed; it does not slide off or fall away. This, then, is how the understanding should pour itself out and spread: never pouring away, but stretching out. It should not crash violently or headlong into the obstacles in its way; nor should it fall down, but stay fixed and light up whatever receives it. For a body that does not let the light in deprives itself of the light.

58. Whoever fears death fears either losing all sensation or having a different kind of sensation. But if you have no sensation, you will not feel any harm either; and if you gain another kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of living being, and you will not stop living.
59. Human beings exist for the sake of one another. So teach them, or bear with them.
60. An arrow moves in one way, the mind in another. Yet the mind, both when it is being cautious and when it is busy examining something, moves straight ahead all the same, toward its target.
61. Enter into every person's ruling faculty; and let every other person enter into yours as well.
